section.title: The Sealed Agreement
section.sectionRationale: Flowing straight out of the great confession of chapter nine, the people now put their commitment in writing. A long roll of names, the governor, the priests, the Levites, and the leaders of the people, is fixed to a sealed document; then the whole community binds itself with a sworn oath to keep God's law in the concrete details of life: marriage, Sabbath, the seventh year, and the ongoing support of the temple through tax, wood, firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes. It is one movement in which repentance takes the shape of a signed, specific covenant.
section.thesis: Genuine repentance does not stop at feeling; it commits itself in writing and in the specifics of ordinary life, so the renewed people bind themselves by oath to keep the Law and, above all, resolve that they will not neglect the house of their God.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the governor and priests who sealed the document; the Levites and leaders who joined them; the binding oath against mixed marriage and for the Sabbath and seventh year; the temple tax and the wood offering; and firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes, closing on the vow not to neglect the house of God.

units.label: The governor and the priests seal the document
units.note: these were the ones who sealed

verses.text: Now these were the ones who sealed the document: Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, and also Zedekiah,
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.

units.label: The Levites and the leaders of the people join them
units.note: the covenant belongs to the whole community

verses.text: The Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel,
and their associates: Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
And the leaders of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani,

units.label: The binding oath: marriage, Sabbath, and the seventh year
units.note: a sworn oath to follow the Law of God

verses.text: “The rest of the people, the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the people of the land to obey the Law of God, along with their wives and all their sons and daughters who are able to understand,

hereby join with their noble brothers and commit themselves with a sworn {{alah|oath}} to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses and to obey carefully all the commandments, ordinances, and statutes of the LORD our Lord.
We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons.

When the people of the land bring merchandise or any kind of grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day. Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt.

units.label: The temple tax and the wood offering
units.note: obligation for the service of God's house

verses.text: We also place ourselves under the obligation to contribute a third of a shekel yearly for the service of the {{beth-elohenu|house of our God}}:

for the showbread, for the regular grain offerings and burnt offerings, for the Sabbath offerings, for the New Moons and appointed feasts, for the holy offerings, for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the duties of the house of our God.

We have cast lots among the priests, Levites, and people for the donation of wood by our families at the appointed times each year. They are to bring it to the house of our God to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.

units.label: Firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes
units.note: we will not neglect the house of our God

verses.text: We will also bring the {{bikkurim|firstfruits}} of our land and of every fruit tree to the house of the LORD year by year.

And we will bring the firstborn of our sons and our livestock, as it is written in the Law, and will bring the firstborn of our herds and flocks to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God.

Moreover, we will bring to the priests at the storerooms of the house of our God the firstfruits of our dough, of our grain offerings, of the fruit of all our trees, and of our new wine and oil. A tenth of our produce belongs to the Levites, so that they shall receive tithes in all the towns where we labor.
A priest of Aaron’s line is to accompany the Levites when they collect the tenth, and the Levites are to bring a tenth of these tithes to the storerooms of the treasury in the house of our God.

For the Israelites and the Levites are to bring the contributions of grain, new wine, and oil to the storerooms where the articles of the sanctuary are kept and where the ministering priests, the gatekeepers, and the singers stay. Thus we will not neglect the house of our God.”

alah.gloss: A solemn oath that carries a self-invoked curse if broken. The people do not merely resolve to do better; they bind themselves under oath, calling down covenant sanctions on themselves if they fail. It shows how seriously they took obedience, and how weighty a vow before God really is.

beth-elohenu.gloss: The house of our God, the temple. This phrase drums through the chapter as the covenant's center of gravity; nearly every commitment, tax, wood, firstfruits, firstborn, and tithe, exists so that worship at God's house will not fail. The whole oath ends on the resolve not to neglect it.

bikkurim.gloss: Firstfruits, the first and best of the harvest, brought to the LORD before the rest is used. To give God the first, not the leftovers, was to confess that all the produce, and the giver, belong to Him. It anticipates Christ, called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

basic.context: After the confession and worship of chapter nine, the people put their repentance in writing. Nehemiah the governor, then the priests, the Levites, and the leaders of the people, set their seal to a formal document. Then the whole community, down to the wives and children old enough to understand, binds itself with a sworn oath to keep the Law of Moses. The oath then gets specific: no intermarriage with the idolatrous peoples of the land, no buying and selling on the Sabbath, keeping the seventh-year rest and debt release, and providing for the temple through a yearly tax, wood for the altar, firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes. It all ends on one ringing line: we will not neglect the house of our God.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative that shows repentance becoming concrete. The particular laws here, the Sabbath market, the temple tax, the wood offering, belong to Israel under the old covenant and are not rules to transfer directly to us. What endures is the pattern: real turning to God shapes marriage, money, work, rest, and worship, not just feelings. The ban on intermarriage is about spiritual fidelity, not race; the danger was being pulled back into idolatry.
basic.originalLanguages: The people commit themselves with an alah, a sworn oath that calls down a curse on covenant-breakers, which is why this is no light promise. The phrase beth elohenu, the house of our God, echoes again and again as the heart of the whole agreement. And they pledge the bikkurim, the firstfruits, the first and best of the harvest, given to God before anything else.
basic.typology: The oath to keep the whole Law, which Israel could never fully perform, points ahead to the one who does keep it perfectly. The firstfruits given to God point to Christ, the firstfruits of the resurrection. And the endless temple offerings for atonement point to the single, final sacrifice He would make.
basic.christ: This chapter shows a people binding themselves by oath to keep a law they will, in fact, break again by the end of the book. That very failure drives the story toward Christ, the one who keeps the law we cannot, and who, under the new covenant, writes it not on a sealed scroll but on the heart. Their care that the house of God not be neglected finds its answer in Him, who is Himself the true temple and the final sacrifice.
basic.god: God is worthy of an obedience that reaches into every corner of life, and He graciously receives a people who commit themselves to Him. Yet the chapter also quietly exposes the limit of human resolve: sincere vows are not the same as a changed heart. God is the one who must ultimately keep His people faithful.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant written on the heart. Hebrews 8 declares that new covenant arrived in Christ. Deuteronomy 7 gives the command against intermarriage with idolaters that stands behind verse 30. And 1 Corinthians 15 names Christ the firstfruits.
basic.oneStory: Repentance takes visible shape here in a signed, specific covenant to keep God's law and support His house. But the very solemnity of the oath sets up the deeper need: a people who cannot keep their word need a Savior who keeps His, and a new covenant that writes the law within. The story runs from this sealed scroll to the cross, where Christ secures the obedience the people could only promise.

context.literary:
This chapter completes a three part covenant renewal that spans chapters eight through ten, the Law is read aloud, chapter eight, the nation confesses its history in prayer, chapter nine, and now that confession is ratified in a signed, sealed document with its stipulations spelled out in concrete detail. The pattern mirrors, on a smaller post exilic scale, the shape of Israel's oldest covenant ceremonies, a recital of God's acts followed by specific obligations and a formal ratification, the same three movements found at Sinai, Exodus 19 to 24, and at Shechem under Joshua, Joshua 24.

The chapter itself falls into two unequal halves joined by one pivotal verse. Verses 1 to 27 are a third person list, first the sealing priests, then the Levites, then the lay leaders, dozens of names with no commentary at all. At verse 28 the voice shifts abruptly to first person plural, we will not give our daughters, we will bring, we will not neglect, and stays there to the end, so that the anonymous roll call of names becomes a living, speaking body binding itself by its own words rather than merely being described from outside.

Running through that second half like a drumbeat is one repeated phrase, the house of our God, appearing five times in twelve verses, verses 32, 33, 34, 36, and 38, functioning almost as a refrain that gathers every separate obligation, tax, wood, firstfruits, firstborn, tithe, under a single controlling purpose, and setting up the chapter's own closing line as its logical, inevitable conclusion.
context.historical:
The temple tax pledged here, a third of a shekel yearly, verse 32, is smaller than the half shekel every Israelite once paid as atonement money whenever the nation was numbered, Exodus 30:13. Scholars have long noticed the difference and generally read it as a fresh, voluntary commitment fitted to a smaller, economically strained community rather than a repeat of the wilderness census tax, evidence that the returned exiles were adapting inherited law to real, present circumstances rather than reenacting it woodenly.

A sealed document naming dozens of specific signatories, priests first, then Levites, then lay leaders, was a recognized legal form in the ancient Near East, comparable to treaty tablets bearing witness lists, and such formality mattered enormously in a small, vulnerable province still rebuilding its institutions from very little. Naming names publicly made the commitment enforceable and shameable, a solemn oath that invoked covenant curses on anyone who broke it, not a private resolution easily forgotten.

The chapter's specific concerns, intermarriage, Sabbath trade, the sabbatical year, and temple support, read like a direct response to failures Ezra and Nehemiah had each already confronted elsewhere in their memoirs; Ezra had dealt with mixed marriages a decade or so earlier, Ezra 9 and 10, and Nehemiah himself would later have to enforce several of these same commitments a second time, Nehemiah 13, evidence that this sealed agreement, however sincere, addressed problems that kept resurfacing in the small province's daily life under a foreign empire that offered little economic margin for costly obedience.
context.canonical:
Nearly every specific clause in this chapter answers to an older law. The tithe for the Levites, verses 37 and 38, restates Numbers 18:21, which gave Israel's priestly tribe the tenth of the harvest as their whole inheritance since they received no allotted land. The sabbatical year rest for fields and cancellation of debts, verse 31, restates Leviticus 25:1 to 7 and Deuteronomy 15:1 and 2, laws so neglected before the exile that Chronicles blames their neglect for the length of the exile itself, the land finally enjoying the sabbaths it was denied, 2 Chronicles 36:21. The ban on intermarriage, verse 30, restates Deuteronomy 7:1 to 4 almost word for word.

This is therefore less a new covenant than a fresh, sworn commitment to obey covenants already long given, a communal act of catching up on obedience owed for generations. Read forward, the story does not end well, Malachi, prophesying perhaps within a generation of this scene, charges the very same community with robbing God by withholding these same tithes, Malachi 3:8 to 10, and Nehemiah's own later governorship finds Sabbath trading and neglected Levites again, Nehemiah 13:10 to 18, the specific vows of this chapter already broken. That repeated failure across the rest of the canon is exactly what makes Jeremiah's promise of a covenant written on the heart, rather than merely signed on a scroll, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, the story's necessary next chapter, fulfilled at last in the covenant Hebrews says Christ now mediates, Hebrews 8:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Nehemiah shapes this scene to show that genuine repentance is verifiable rather than merely felt. A vague resolve to do better could not be checked by anyone; a specific, signed pledge naming exact percentages, exact gates, and exact categories of produce can be checked, by the very community that made it and by every generation of readers since. The specificity is the point, it resists the natural tendency for pious feeling to evaporate once the emotional moment of confession, chapter nine, has passed.

The repeated phrase as it is written in the Law, verses 34 and 36, also reveals authorial intent to root every new obligation in Moses rather than in fresh, self authorized religious invention. The author wants this reforming community understood as restorers of an old covenant, not founders of a new religion, guarding the returned exiles' legitimacy as heirs of Israel's ancient faith even while living, landless and kingless, inside someone else's empire. Naming signatories by office, governor, priests, Levites, leaders, further intends to fix accountability at every level of the community, so that no single group could later claim the vow was never truly theirs.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The exact figures here, a third of a shekel rather than Exodus's half shekel, one specific rotation of wood bearing families, are historically conditioned details describing how one particular community met its particular obligations; they are not a permanent percentage or schedule binding on believers in every era. What Scripture treats as unchanging is the underlying principle each figure serves, that God's gathered worship deserves regular, planned, sacrificial support rather than leftover or occasional giving.

Likewise the ban on intermarriage describes a specific application of covenant loyalty to a community surrounded by idolatrous neighbors; it is not a timeless command against marriage across ethnic lines as such, since Scripture elsewhere welcomes believing outsiders like Ruth into full covenant standing. The enduring principle is singular devotion, guarding against relationships that would pull a believer's worship toward rival gods, a concern the New Testament restates directly rather than by ethnicity, do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers, 2 Corinthians 6:14.

debates.question: Was the ban on intermarriage in verse 30 about race or about faith?

views.label: Spiritual fidelity, not ethnicity
views.case: The concern throughout Ezra and Nehemiah is the peoples of the land whose idolatry had drawn Israel away before; foreigners who embraced the LORD, like Ruth the Moabitess, were fully welcomed. The issue is being bound to unbelief and its gods, not ethnic purity.

views.label: Preserving the distinct covenant people
views.case: There is also real concern to keep the returned remnant separate and consecrated, a people set apart to God through whom the promise would come; yet even this separateness was defined by covenant loyalty rather than by blood.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on the New Testament principle of not being unequally yoked with unbelief, and both serve the coming of Christ, in whom people of every nation are gathered by faith.

debates.question: How should we read a solemn oath to keep the whole Law?

views.label: A sincere and commendable act of repentance
views.case: The people are responding rightly to God's word and grace; binding themselves to obedience in the specifics of life is exactly what true repentance looks like, and Scripture commends it.

views.label: A revealing of the limits of human resolve
views.case: By the end of Nehemiah the very commitments made here are broken again, showing that vows, however sincere, cannot by themselves produce a faithful heart; the episode exposes the need for a deeper, inward covenant.

debates.bearing: Held together, the two point forward: the pledge is good and right, yet it drives the story toward the new covenant in which God writes His law on the heart and Christ keeps it on our behalf.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words beyond those the basic level already names carry the chapter's argument forward. The closing vow, we will not neglect the house of our God, verse 39, uses the same root that recurs as a refrain across chapter nine, You did not forsake them, verses 17, 19, 28, and 31. The link is almost certainly deliberate, what God refused to do to a rebellious people across a thousand years of history, they now solemnly refuse to do to His house. The prayer confessed God's not forsaking; the oath answers with the community's own not forsaking, and the whole covenant renewal turns on that verbal echo binding the two chapters into a single movement.

The sabbatical commitment of verse 31, every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt, names a specific institution built on the verb to let drop or release, the very term Deuteronomy 15 uses for debt cancellation. That this law needed a fresh, sworn commitment at all is itself an admission that Israel had simply not kept it; the sabbatical year appears nowhere as an observed practice earlier in the historical books, and its neglect is even blamed, in 2 Chronicles 36:21, for the length of the exile itself, the land finally enjoying its sabbaths by force once the people would not give them willingly.

The tithe pledged in verses 37 and 38, the tenth, is not a new tax the community invents but the ancient portion Numbers 18:21 assigns the Levites as their entire inheritance in place of land; naming it here ties the post exilic community's obedience directly back to wilderness legislation centuries old, insisting this is restoration, not innovation.

And the lots cast for the wood offering, verse 34, are the same word that will decide, one chapter later, who moves into Jerusalem itself, Nehemiah 11:1; the community that here casts lots to fairly share a burden of fuel for the altar will shortly cast the identical kind of lot to fairly share the far heavier burden of living inside the exposed holy city, the same procedure serving both a minor logistical need and a major, costly calling.

Taken together these four terms, forsake, release, tithe, and lot, show a document far more woven into the rest of Scripture's vocabulary than a first reading suggests, each word reaching back to a specific earlier law or forward to a specific later chapter, so that the community's oath is less an isolated burst of zeal than one more knot tied into a rope of covenant language running the length of the whole Hebrew Bible.

typology.type: The oath to keep the whole Law of Moses
typology.fulfillment: Six hundred and more specific commandments, the very ones this document swears to obey carefully, describe a standard no one who signed it, or their children, would keep without fail, as Galatians states plainly, cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law, Galatians 3:10. Jesus alone comes not to abolish that law but to fulfill it in every jot and stroke, Matthew 5:17 and 18, and what the law, weakened by human flesh, could never produce, God accomplished by sending His Son, so that the law's righteous standard is now fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, Romans 8:3 and 4. The type falls short in that Israel's oath could only bind the will; Christ's obedience actually satisfies the standard, and His Spirit now enables what mere signatures could not.

typology.type: The firstfruits brought to the house of God
typology.fulfillment: The firstfruits of field and tree, brought before the rest of the harvest is touched, confess that the whole yield, and the one bringing it, belong to God. Paul takes up the identical picture for the resurrection, Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and just as the firstfruits guaranteed the coming harvest, His resurrection guarantees that those who belong to Him will also be raised at His coming, 1 Corinthians 15:23. The escalation is that Nehemiah's firstfruits were consumed and gone each year, needing to be brought again and again, while Christ, the once for all firstfruits, need never be offered twice.

typology.type: The temple offerings and sin offerings that make atonement
typology.fulfillment: Showbread, grain offerings, burnt offerings, and above all the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, verse 33, kept the temple's altar in constant use, an endless rhythm of blood that had to be repeated because it could never actually remove sin, only cover it for a time. Hebrews contrasts that very endlessness with Christ, day after day every priest stands to minister and offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, but this Priest, after one sacrifice for sins, sat down, because a single offering made perfect for all time those being sanctified, Hebrews 10:11 to 14. The temple's altar never stopped needing fuel; Christ's one sacrifice ended the need for more.

typology.type: The law sealed on an outward document
typology.fulfillment: A written, sealed scroll can record a community's intention, but it cannot change the will that must keep reading and obeying it, and by the end of this very book several of its own clauses lie broken, Nehemiah 13. Jeremiah had already promised the answer before this covenant was even signed, a covenant unlike the one their fathers broke, in which God's law is placed in their minds and written on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, a promise Hebrews says is now founded, the first, aging arrangement made obsolete, Hebrews 8:8 to 13. Where verse 39's oath depended entirely on human resolve holding firm, the new covenant depends on God Himself doing the writing, on the inside rather than the outside.

study.christ:
Verse 30's pledge, we will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, guards Israel's holiness by exclusion, a boundary drawn around ethnic and religious lines to keep the covenant people from being absorbed into the nations. Paul draws on the same instinct when he tells the church not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, 2 Corinthians 6:14, yet the boundary itself is transformed in Christ, the marriage that finally matters is not one Israel must protect by excluding outsiders but one in which the Lamb takes a bride gathered out of every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, Revelation 5:9 and 19:7. What this chapter guards by keeping foreigners out, the gospel fulfills by bringing them in, on the single new condition of faith rather than descent.

The seventh year pledge to cancel every debt, verse 31, a law Israel had evidently let lapse for generations, points toward a cancellation this book's community could offer only its neighbors and only every seventh year. Christ answers a debt no sabbatical cycle could reach, the accusing record of everything written against us, and nails it to the cross, canceling it once, permanently, rather than every seven years, Colossians 2:14. The prayer Jesus taught His disciples, forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, Matthew 6:12, asks for exactly this kind of release, the very language this chapter's sabbatical pledge anticipates but cannot itself supply.

Even the small detail of the temple tax carries a quiet Christological weight. Centuries later, when tax collectors ask whether Jesus pays the temple tax, He asks Peter whose sons pay tribute, their own or foreigners, establishing that as the Son He owes nothing to His Father's house, yet He still has a coin drawn from a fish's mouth to pay it for both of them, so as not to offend, Matthew 17:24 to 27. The very obligation this chapter's third of a shekel establishes, He is exempt from by right and yet meets anyway, in a small enacted parable of how He fulfills what He owes nothing toward, for the sake of others.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who cares intensely about the ordinary mechanics of worship staying funded and staffed, not only about the sentiment behind it. A third of a shekel yearly, a rotation of families bringing wood, a priest of Aaron's line assigned specifically to accompany the Levites when they collect the tenth, verse 38, all describe a system built for accountability, so that no single group handles God's provisions unsupervised. A God this careful about how money and produce for His house are collected and checked is a God who takes financial integrity in worship seriously, the same concern Paul later voices when he arranges for reputable men to travel with the collection for Jerusalem so that no one can blame him in the way this gift is administered, 2 Corinthians 8:20 and 21.

The sabbatical pledge, letting fields lie fallow and debts go free every seventh year, verse 31, reveals a God whose care reaches beyond the human community to the land itself and to the economically vulnerable within it; the ground is not merely a resource to be exploited without limit, and debt is not meant to become a permanent chain. That this law had evidently gone unpracticed for generations, only now being freshly sworn, shows a God patient enough to keep pressing an old command rather than quietly letting it drop once a people has shown it will not easily obey.

Above all, God is the one all these gifts ultimately belong to before they are ever given. Firstfruits, firstborn, and tithe are not really donations to a needy deity but returns to the rightful owner, an implicit theology running through the entire chapter, the land, the harvest, the flock, and even the firstborn son belong to the LORD first, and human households merely hold them for a time. A God who requires that the first and best come back to Him is not extracting tribute from reluctant subjects; He is simply being acknowledged as the giver of everything the community is now returning in thanksgiving.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah promises a covenant unlike the one Israel's fathers broke, one in which God writes His law on the heart rather than a scroll, and forgives iniquity permanently. The sworn, sealed document of Nehemiah 10 is exactly the kind of external covenant that promise supersedes, since even sincere signatures cannot supply the inward change Jeremiah describes.

Hebrews declares that new covenant now founded in Christ, mediated on better promises than the first covenant Israel kept breaking. The very sealing and swearing recorded here belongs to that first, aging covenant, sincere and valuable, yet destined to be surpassed by one that does not depend on human resolve holding firm.

The command against intermarrying with the nations, lest they turn Israel's children after other gods, stands directly behind the pledge of verse 30. The concern is never ethnic but religious, keeping covenant loyalty from being diluted by household gods brought in through marriage.

Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, the guarantee that the full harvest of resurrection will follow. The firstfruits pledged to God's house in Nehemiah 10:35 are a small, repeated shadow of that one, unrepeatable firstfruits offering.

Malachi charges the whole nation with robbing God by withholding tithes and offerings, promising overflowing blessing if the full tithe is brought into the storehouse instead. The very obligation sworn here in good faith is precisely what Malachi's generation, not long after, would be accused of neglecting.

Every Israelite once paid a half shekel as atonement money for his life whenever the nation was numbered. Nehemiah's community instead pledges a third of a shekel yearly for the ongoing service of the temple, a related but distinct obligation, showing how a wilderness ordinance was adapted to a smaller community's fresh, voluntary commitment.

Leviticus first commands a Sabbath rest for the land itself every seventh year, with no sowing or reaping, so that even the ground shares in God's pattern of rest. The pledge of verse 31 to let the fields lie fallow answers a command Israel had evidently neglected across the centuries before the exile.

Numbers assigns the Levites the tithe of Israel as their whole inheritance, since they receive no allotted land, in return for their service at the tent of meeting. Nehemiah 10:37 and 38 renew that ancient arrangement almost verbatim, insisting on continuity with Moses rather than any new invention.

Within the same book, Nehemiah later finds the Levites' portions withheld and traders openly selling on the Sabbath, the very commitments sworn here broken in the details. The juxtaposition is sobering, showing how quickly even a solemn, sealed oath can be neglected once its first fervor cools.

study.oneStory:
Every strand of this chapter answers a question the rest of the Bible keeps asking in different words, once God has rescued a people, how are they meant to live together as His, in the actual texture of marriage, money, work, rest, and the upkeep of worship. Genesis already showed a good creation given order, work, and a Sabbath rhythm before sin entered it; this chapter is a small, late attempt to recover exactly that ordered rhythm, fields resting, debts released, the first and best returned to God, inside a world sin has otherwise bent out of shape.

The specific shape of the pledge, no marriage into the surrounding nations, tithes for the Levites, wood for the altar, gathers up commands scattered across Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy and binds them into one fresh act of obedience, showing this small province still sees itself bound to the whole of Moses rather than picking a convenient fragment. That impulse to gather the whole law into a single answering vow is itself part of the story arc running from Sinai's giving of that same law to the day a greater than Moses would fulfill it entirely rather than merely swear to it.

But the story does not end satisfied. Malachi will soon accuse this very community's grandchildren of robbing God through the withheld tithes this chapter swears to bring, and Nehemiah's own later return, chapter 13, finds Sabbath trading and neglected Levites, the specific vows of this chapter already broken. The unresolved ache is the same one that runs through every covenant renewal from Sinai onward, obedience promised in good faith and not sustained, and it keeps the whole story reaching forward, past this chapter, past this book, toward a covenant that does not depend on a community's resolve holding firm across even one more generation, let alone across the centuries this history keeps proving too long for merely human faithfulness.

sermon.title: Renewing the Covenant for the Sake of God's Name
sermon.why: Piper preaches on the covenant reaffirmation and the sealed document with the names of leaders, Levites, and priests, the very act recorded in Nehemiah 10, showing that such a covenant is only possible because God is abundantly gracious and steadfast in love. A fitting, gospel-centered handling of this movement's sealed agreement.

quiz.q: What did the people do first as the fruit of their confession?

options.text: They put their commitment in writing, and their leaders sealed a formal document.
options.note: Verses 1-27 record the governor, priests, Levites, and leaders sealing the covenant.

options.text: They immediately rebuilt the temple from the ground up.
options.note: The temple already stood; the fresh act here was sealing a written covenant, not rebuilding.

options.text: They appointed a new king over Judah.
options.note: There was no new king; Judah was under Persian rule and led by Nehemiah the governor.

options.text: They abandoned the Law of Moses.
options.note: The opposite; they bound themselves by oath to obey the Law of Moses.

quiz.q: What kind of commitment did the people make in verse 29?

options.text: A sworn oath, binding themselves under God to follow the Law given through Moses.
options.note: The Hebrew alah is a solemn oath that carries a self-invoked curse on those who break it.

options.text: A casual, non-binding suggestion to try harder.
options.note: It was far more than a suggestion; it was a formal, sworn, binding oath.

options.text: A promise binding only on the priests.
options.note: The oath included the whole community, down to wives and children old enough to understand.

options.text: A vow to keep only the laws they found convenient.
options.note: They swore to obey carefully all the commandments, ordinances, and statutes.

quiz.q: Why did the covenant forbid marriage with the peoples of the land?

options.text: To guard against being drawn back into their idolatry, the very sin that had led to exile.
options.note: The concern was spiritual fidelity; foreigners who embraced the LORD, like Ruth, were welcomed.

options.text: To keep the bloodline ethnically pure for its own sake.
options.note: The issue was covenant loyalty, not race; the danger was idolatry, not ethnicity.

options.text: Because marriage itself was regarded as unclean.
options.note: Marriage was honored; the danger was being unequally yoked to idol worship.

options.text: Because Persian law required it.
options.note: It flowed from God's command in the Law, not from Persian law.

quiz.q: What single resolve does the covenant end on in verse 39?

options.text: We will not neglect the house of our God.
options.note: The whole oath climaxes on this vow to keep the temple and its worship supplied.

options.text: We will build a wall around every city in Judah.
options.note: The wall was built earlier; the covenant's closing vow concerns the house of God, not walls.

options.text: We will conquer the surrounding nations.
options.note: There is no pledge of conquest; the focus is faithful worship and giving.

options.text: We will never again offer any sacrifices.
options.note: The opposite; they committed to sustaining the offerings at the temple.

quiz.q: How does this sealed covenant point us toward Christ?

options.text: It shows a people who cannot finally keep their oath, driving the story toward the one who keeps the law and writes it on the heart.
options.note: By the end of Nehemiah the vows are broken, revealing the need for the new covenant in Christ, Jeremiah 31 and Hebrews 8.

options.text: It proves that sincere vows alone are enough to make a heart faithful.
options.note: The book shows the opposite; the very commitments here are later broken.

options.text: It teaches that God no longer cares about obedience.
options.note: God cares deeply about obedience; the point is that Christ secures what we cannot.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ or the gospel.
options.note: The firstfruits, the sacrifices, and the promised law-keeper all point to Christ.

questions: The people turned their confession into something written and specific. Where is God calling you to move from vague good intentions to concrete, named commitments?
Their oath reached into marriage, money, work, and rest, not just their feelings. Which ordinary corner of your life most needs to be brought under God's lordship right now?
They gave God the firstfruits, the first and best, rather than the leftovers. What would it look like for God to have the first of your time, energy, and money instead of what remains?
The whole covenant circled around not neglecting the house of God. How are you tempted to let the worship and life of God's people slip down your list of priorities?
By the end of the book these very vows were broken. How does knowing that Christ keeps the law we cannot, and writes it on our hearts, change the way you pursue obedience this week?

translationNotes.note: In the Hebrew text the verse numbering differs; what English Bibles print as Nehemiah 9:38 begins the covenant here, so some editions start chapter 10 one verse earlier. The content, the sealed document and its signatories, is the same.
The temple servants render the Hebrew Nethinim, a class of assistants attached to the temple; the BSB footnote gives the Hebrew term.

A third of a shekel is roughly 3.8 grams, probably of silver; the BSB footnote gives the weight. It differs from the half-shekel of Exodus 30, likely reflecting the economic strain of the small post-exilic community.
Cancel every debt renders the seventh-year release of Deuteronomy 15; together with letting the fields lie fallow it keeps the sabbatical-year law that Israel had long ignored.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Nehemiah 10:1-39. All 39 verses present in order. Sermon verified this session: John Piper, Desiring God, on the covenant reaffirmation and sealed document of Nehemiah 9:38 to 10.
